docs.title: intel enrichment cache
docs.text:
A threat intelligence client for a SOAR worker, built around the constraint that actually bites: a free tier allows a few hundred lookups a day, and an alert pipeline produces more than that before lunch.

So the library is organised as a series of stages that each stop work reaching the next, and the only interesting measurement is how much work never becomes a request.

from iec import EnrichmentClient, ProviderBudget, SqliteCache, VirusTotal, preset

client = EnrichmentClient(
    [ProviderBudget.from_preset(VirusTotal(api_key), preset("virustotal-public"))],
    cache=SqliteCache("intel-cache.sqlite"),
    quota="intel-quota.sqlite",
)

verdict = await client.enrich("8.8.8.8")
print(verdict.disposition, verdict.source)

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• Measurements is what the cache, the coalescer and the hedger are each worth, and which of those figures are simulated.
  • Where the numbers come from separates the three kinds of figure in this repository: limits read from a vendor's documentation, choices this library made, and things that were measured.
  • Limitations is what it does not do, each with the condition that would trigger building it.
  • The decision records include one that publishes a measurement arguing against its own conclusion, and one about the four separate ways the benchmark was wrong before it was believable.

docs.title: The design in one paragraph
docs.text: Five stages, cheapest first: a cache read, a dictionary lookup to collapse concurrent duplicates, a durable quota check that refuses before anything leaves the process, a token bucket that paces what does leave, and finally the request. Errors are never cached, because an error is a fact about the network rather than about the indicator. A partial answer is returned rather than discarded, because an analyst holding one verdict and a note about the other source is better served than one holding an exception. The worst verdict wins, because averaging a detection with an absence of one produces a number that means nothing.

docs.title: The thing most libraries get wrong
docs.text:
Hedging. Sending a duplicate request when the first is slow is close to free against an unmetered service and is not free against a metered one, so a hedge here has to clear three gates: the first request is still outstanding, a token is free without waiting, and enough of the daily allowance remains. Below the floor the hedge is refused, because the last of the budget belongs to alerts with no answer at all rather than to a faster answer for one already on its way.

This library's own docstring was wrong about the size of that cost until the benchmark corrected it, which is written up in measurements rather than quietly fixed.

docs.title: What this does not do
docs.text: Each entry says what would trigger building it, so the list is a set of decisions rather than a set of excuses.

docs.title: A shared quota ledger
docs.text:
The ledger is a SQLite file. Two workers pointed at the same file coordinate correctly, because the write path takes the lock before it counts. Two workers on different volumes do not, and will each spend the full allowance of a key they share.

This is the limitation to fix first, ahead of the shared cache below. Two workers sharing a key already share an allowance, so the ledger has to be shared before the cache does, and getting that ordering backwards means a distributed cache that still gets the key suspended.

Trigger: a second worker that cannot see the first one's volume.

docs.title: A shared cache
docs.text:
The Cache protocol is narrow on purpose, so a distributed backend is a swap rather than a rewrite. Until then, two workers each hold their own cache and each miss on indicators the other has already fetched, at which point a per worker cache has stopped being a cache and become two.

Trigger: the same second worker. See ADR-002 for why that trigger is a second worker rather than a traffic volume.

docs.title: Lifetime from the verdict rather than the class
docs.text:
A harmless verdict going stale is what costs a detection; a malicious one going stale costs nothing, because nobody ever regretted treating a known bad indicator as bad for an extra week. So lifetimes arguably belong on the disposition and not only on the indicator class, and that is a better idea than the one implemented.

It needs evidence about how often a harmless verdict flips, which this project does not have. ADR-001 is explicit that no replay of an indicator stream can supply it: the stream records what was looked up, not what the answer would have been at other times.

Trigger: a corpus of verdicts for the same indicators over time, from which a flip rate can be measured rather than assumed.

docs.title: Freshness from the provider
docs.text:
Both providers return information about when they last analysed an indicator, which is a better freshness signal than any policy in this library. Not used, because it makes the cache depend on the shape of a response field outside this project's control, and doing that defensively is a larger change than it looks.

Trigger: a second opinion on how stable those fields are, or a provider whose published contract covers them.

docs.title: Retries
docs.text:
There are none. A provider error is reported, not retried. A retry on a metered API is a second request, so it belongs to the same budget as a hedge and deserves the same treatment: a policy with a quota floor, rather than a loop. The structure for that exists, in hedging.py, and has not been generalised.

What the library does instead is make a single failure cheap to handle: the error reaches every coalesced waiter from one attempt rather than each of them retrying, and a partial answer from one provider is returned rather than discarded because another failed.

Trigger: a provider whose documented error rate makes one attempt insufficient, measured rather than assumed.

docs.title: Rate limit reconciliation from response headers
docs.text:
Retry-After is read where a provider sends it, in the delay seconds form. Nothing adjusts the token bucket from a provider's own remaining quota headers, which would be the only source of truth belonging to the caller rather than to a preset in this repository.

Not implemented because the header names differ per provider and this library should not assert what they are without having read each contract. docs/sources.md records which figures came from documentation and which are this library's own choice.

Trigger: a provider whose documentation specifies its rate limit headers, at which point reconciliation can be written against a contract.

docs.title: Indicator classes beyond four
docs.text:
Addresses, file hashes, domains and URLs. No IPv6, no email addresses, no registry keys, no mutexes. IPv6 is the obvious gap and is absent because the classifier would need to handle its many textual forms, and an indicator sorted into the wrong class gets the wrong cache lifetime and goes to a provider that cannot answer it.

Trigger: IPv6 on first request. The others on evidence anyone enriches them.

docs.title: Submitting anything
docs.text:
Both provider clients are read only by construction: no upload, no report, no vote. That is not a limitation to be fixed. An analyst calling an enrichment function does not expect a copy of a customer's file to leave the building, or their own egress address to be published as an abuser.

Trigger: none. A separate library, if anyone wants one.

docs.title: Measurements
docs.text: Generated by tools/generate_measurements_doc.py from docs/metrics.json. Reproduce the whole thing with make bench.

docs.title: The stream these numbers come from
docs.text:
Generated, not captured: a Zipf repeat distribution at alpha 1.1 over a universe 20% the length of the stream, arriving in bursts of 8 on average spread over 2 seconds, across a simulated 7 days.

Members of a burst draw indicators independently from the Zipf distribution rather than sharing a dominant one. A real scan burst is dominated by the indicator that caused it, so this understates coalescing rather than flattering it.

docs.title: Real: what the cache and the coalescer are worth
docs.text:
No latency model is involved in these. A request count is a property of the algorithm on a stated stream and does not depend on how long a request takes, so the experiment that produces them removes latency entirely.

lookups days cache hit rate coalesced requests per 1,000 lookups a free tier supports 10,000 7.0 0.544 112 444.5 1,125 a day 100,000 7.0 0.676 190 322.5 1,550 a day

The last column is the point of the library. VirusTotal's public tier allows 500 requests a day, so an uncached client enriches 500 indicators a day and then stops. At the measured request rate the same allowance covers about 1,550 lookups a day, which is 3.1 times as many.

docs.title: Real: what a cache lifetime policy costs
docs.text:
policy cache hit rate requests per 1,000 lookups per_class_defaults 0.643 353.5 uniform_1h 0.512 481.8 uniform_4h 0.642 355.7 uniform_24h 0.780 219.2 uniform_7d 0.889 110.6

A uniform 7d lifetime reaches a 0.889 hit rate against 0.643 for the per class defaults, at 3.2 times fewer requests. On hit rate alone the per class policy loses decisively, which is why hit rate is the wrong criterion: a longer lifetime always scores better, up to never expiring anything, which would score perfectly and be useless. What this table measures is the price of the safety, and ADR-001 is the argument about whether to pay it.

docs.title: Simulated: what hedging buys and costs
docs.text:
The latency figures below are a simulation. There is no API behind them. They come from a lognormal body with a median of 180ms and sigma 0.45, plus 2% of responses stalling at 12 times the median, and they are only as good as that model. The request counts in the same table are real.

policy p50 p95 p99 requests extra requests p99 change off 192ms 430ms 2328ms 1,490 +0.00% +0.0% after_400ms 191ms 432ms 598ms 1,575 +5.70% -74.3% after_800ms 193ms 432ms 970ms 1,518 +1.88% -58.3% after_1500ms 192ms 431ms 1658ms 1,514 +1.61% -28.8%

Percentiles are nearest rank over 1,490 lookups, so the p99 is the 15th slowest observation rather than an interpolation between two that were never seen.

The module's own docstring used to argue that hedging is expensive on a metered API. It is not: a hedge only fires on a request that has already stalled, so its cost is bounded by the 2% stall rate rather than by the traffic. Hedging after 400ms cut the simulated p99 by 74% for 5.7% more requests. The docstring now says so.

It is still off by default. 5% more requests is cheap and it is still 5% a caller did not ask for, and the stall rate it depends on belongs to somebody else's service: a provider having a bad hour is exactly when the stall rate climbs, which is exactly when the budget can least absorb it. That is what the quota floor is for.

docs.title: What is not measured here
docs.text: How long a verdict stays true, which is the thing that would settle the cache lifetime defaults. No replay of an indicator stream can supply it: the stream records what was looked up, not what the answer would have been at other times. See limitations.

docs.title: Where the numbers come from
docs.text: Three kinds of figure appear in this repository, and they are not equally trustworthy. Keeping them apart is the point of this file.

docs.title: Documented limits, read from the vendor
docs.text:
figure source read on VirusTotal public API: 4 requests per minute, 500 per day docs.virustotal.com, public versus premium API 2026-10-21 AbuseIPDB standard plan, CHECK endpoint: 1,000 per day docs.abuseipdb.com, rate limits 2026-10-21 AbuseIPDB standard plan, REPORTS endpoint: 100 per day docs.abuseipdb.com, rate limits 2026-10-21

Each is attached to its preset in src/iec/limits/presets.py with the source and the date, so a reader who wants to know whether a figure is still true knows where to look. Every preset also carries verify_against_your_account, because none of them can be checked from inside this library and a caller on a paid tier has different numbers entirely.

docs.title: This library's own choices, labelled as such
docs.text:
AbuseIPDB documents a daily limit for these endpoints and no short window one. The per minute pacing in those presets, 10 for CHECK and 5 for REPORTS, is this library being conservative, not a number the vendor published. Presenting it as theirs would be inventing a fact about somebody else's API, so the preset's note says so and a test asserts the label is present.

The disposition thresholds are also choices: two engines for malicious, one for suspicious, 75 and 25 on AbuseIPDB's confidence scale. The reasoning is in providers/base.py and they are configurable, because a team that buries its analysts on single engine detections should be able to move the line without forking.

The cache lifetime defaults are reasoning rather than measurement, and ADR-001 is explicit that the measurement which would settle them does not exist in this project.

docs.title: Measurements, and which of them are simulated
docs.text:
docs/metrics.json carries a note field recording this, and every key derived from the latency model is suffixed _simulated.

Real. Cache hit rates, coalescing counts, provider request counts, and everything derived from them including requests per thousand lookups and the lookups per day a free tier supports. These are properties of the algorithm on a stated stream. No part of them depends on a latency model, which is why the experiments that produce them use no latency at all.

Simulated. Every latency percentile. There is no API behind them. They come from the lognormal plus stall tail model in benchmark/mock_provider.py, whose parameters are recorded in the metrics file, and they are only as good as that model. The p99 improvement hedging shows is a statement about the model, not a promise about VirusTotal.

Real, inside the simulated experiment. The request counts in the hedging experiment. This matters: hedging's cost is paid in requests and its benefit only in latency, so the half of that trade which is measured rather than modelled is the cost.

docs.title: The stream the measurements run on
docs.text:
Generated, not captured, with every parameter in benchmark/stream.py: a Zipf repeat distribution at alpha 1.1 over a universe one fifth the stream's length, arriving in bursts over a simulated week.

It is a model of alert traffic and not anybody's alert traffic. One choice in it is deliberately conservative: members of a burst draw their indicators independently rather than sharing a dominant one, where a real scan burst is dominated by the indicator that caused it. That understates coalescing rather than flattering it.

A reader wanting their own numbers should replay their own indicator log. That is what stream.load() is for, and it is one line in the benchmark.

docs.title: ADR-001: Lifetime per indicator class, and the measurement that argues against it
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-21

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
A cached verdict is useful until it is wrong. How long that takes depends on what kind of thing was looked up: a file hash verdict changes when a vendor re-scans the sample, which is days or weeks, while an address reputation changes when a host is cleaned up or newly compromised, which is hours.

The planned decision was per class lifetimes over a single global one, and the planned justification was a measured hit rate. The measurement was run and argues the other way.

docs.title: What was measured
docs.text:
10,000 lookups over a simulated week, drawn from a Zipf distribution with alpha 1.1 over a universe one fifth the length of the stream, arriving in bursts. Full parameters in benchmark/stream.py; every figure reproduces with make bench.

lifetime policy cache hit rate provider requests per 1,000 lookups per class defaults 0.572 422 uniform 1 hour 0.393 586 uniform 4 hours 0.554 438 uniform 24 hours 0.732 266 uniform 7 days 0.873 127

A uniform seven day lifetime beats the per class policy on hit rate by a wide margin, and costs a third of the requests. On the criterion the measurement was designed to settle, per class loses decisively.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Per class lifetimes, with the measurement published next to it.

Hit rate is the wrong criterion, and running the measurement is what made that obvious. A longer lifetime always produces a better hit rate, right up to a policy of never expiring anything, which would score perfectly and be useless. What the table measures is not whether the policy is good; it is the price of the policy.

The thing hit rate cannot see is which wrong answers each policy produces. A seven day old harmless verdict on an address that was compromised yesterday is the single most expensive wrong answer this library can give, because it is indistinguishable from a fresh one and it suppresses a real detection in silence. A seven day old verdict on a file hash is usually still true.

So the decision rests on a judgement the benchmark cannot make, and the benchmark's job is to say what the judgement costs: 422 requests per thousand lookups instead of 127, which is 3.3 times the quota, in exchange for never serving an address reputation more than four hours old.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
A team that disagrees can disagree concretely. TTLPolicy takes a dictionary, TTLPolicy.uniform exists specifically so the comparison in the table above is one line to reproduce, and a team willing to accept day old address reputations knows from this table what it buys them.

The defaults themselves are reasoning rather than measurement, and the module docstring says so. Nothing in a replayed indicator stream can reveal how long a verdict stays true, because the stream records what was looked up and not what the answer would have been at other times. Measuring that needs a corpus of verdicts over time, which this project does not have and does not pretend to.

An unknown answer gets its own, shorter lifetime, for a different reason: caching it at all matters because on a long tailed stream the indicators nobody has heard of are where the quota goes, and expiring it sooner matters because an indicator nobody knows today may be known tomorrow, which is the case where staleness costs a detection rather than just a request.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
One global lifetime. Simpler, measurably better on hit rate, and wrong for the reason above. A single value is either too short for hashes, which wastes the quota the cache exists to save, or too long for addresses, which is the dangerous direction.

Lifetime from the verdict rather than the class. Expire a malicious verdict slowly and a harmless one quickly, since a harmless verdict going stale is what costs a detection. This is a better idea than the one implemented and is not implemented: it needs evidence about how often a harmless verdict flips, which is the measurement this project does not have. Recorded in docs/limitations.md with the condition that would trigger it.

Lifetime from provider supplied freshness. Both providers return information about when they last analysed an indicator, which is a better signal than any policy here. Rejected for this version only because it makes the cache depend on a response field whose shape is outside this project's control, and the defensive parsing that would need is a larger change than it looks.

docs.title: ADR-002: SQLite for both the cache and the quota ledger
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-21

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
This library needs two pieces of durable state: the indicator cache and the daily quota ledger. The quota ledger has to be durable rather than in memory, because a worker that restarts and forgets what it spent will spend it again, and the whole point of local accounting is to avoid learning the limit from the provider. The cache does not strictly have to be durable, but a cache that empties on every deploy spends a day's allowance refilling itself.

Redis is the reflexive answer and would work. So would a second store for one of the two.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: SQLite, in WAL mode, for both.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
One fewer service to run, monitor, back up, secure and explain. A SOAR worker is often deployed as a container with a volume, and a library that requires a Redis to be stood up before it can cache anything is a library that does not get adopted for a week while somebody argues about where the Redis lives.

One store rather than two. The quota ledger and the cache have the same durability needs and the same access pattern, and a second technology for the second one would be a second thing to configure and get wrong.

WAL mode, so readers do not block the writer. Several workers against one volume is common enough that the default rollback journal, where a write excludes every reader, would make the cache the contention point it was added to remove.

The quota ledger's write path uses BEGIN IMMEDIATE around the count and the insert. Without it two workers can count the same free slot and both fill it, which is the one place in this library where a race produces an over spend rather than a wasted request.

Cache access goes through a thread, because SQLite's driver is blocking and a coroutine that calls it stalls every other task in the worker. That is a fraction of a millisecond on a local file and easy to shrug at, and it is not a fraction of a millisecond when the file is on network storage or another process holds the write lock. Connections are thread local, not one shared behind a lock, which would serialise reads across the pool and defeat the point of moving them off the loop.

docs.title: What the measurement says about the choice
docs.text:
The benchmark replays 10,000 lookups at roughly 1,100 lookups a second end to end, through the cache, the coalescer and the quota ledger. At the volumes this library is for, where a free tier allows 500 provider requests a day, the store is not within an order of magnitude of being the constraint. The constraint is the provider's allowance, which is the thing the cache exists to stretch.

That is the argument for SQLite being sufficient, and it is not an argument that SQLite is faster than Redis. It is not.

docs.title: The pivot
docs.text:
The Cache protocol in cache/store.py is deliberately narrow: get, put, purge, stats. A distributed backend goes behind it the moment a second enrichment worker exists and the two start missing on indicators the other has already fetched, which is the point at which a per worker cache stops being a cache and becomes two.

The trigger is a second worker, not a volume of traffic. An interface with a SQLite shaped hole in it would make that a rewrite rather than a swap, which is why the protocol has no transaction, no connection and no path in it.

Note that the quota ledger does not have that interface and would need one. Two workers sharing an API key already share an allowance, so the ledger has to be shared before the cache does. That is the honest ordering and it is recorded in docs/limitations.md.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
Redis for both. Rejected on operational cost at the target deployment size, not on capability. It is the right answer at the second worker, which is what the pivot above is for.

In memory for the cache, SQLite for the ledger. A faster cache that empties on deploy. Rejected: a cold cache after every rollout spends a large share of a free tier's daily allowance re-fetching answers it already had, which is the cost this library exists to avoid.

No ledger, rely on the provider's 429. Rejected outright. It means learning the limit by hitting it, the response to which is a request already spent, and on some tiers repeated breaches are what gets a key suspended rather than throttled.

docs.title: ADR-003: One mechanism per experiment, not one harness for all of them
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-10-21

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Three things needed measuring: how many provider requests a stream costs, what a cache lifetime policy is worth, and what hedging buys and costs.

The first attempt drove all three through one general purpose virtual clock, on the reasoning that a single harness is less code than three. It produced numbers that were wrong in four distinct ways before any of them were believable, and finding each one took longer than the measurement it was blocking.

docs.title: What went wrong, in order
docs.text:
No time passed, so lifetimes measured nothing. The first version submitted every alert at once. Virtual time then only advanced by the simulated request latency, so a ten thousand alert replay covered about a minute, no cache entry ever expired, and all five lifetime policies scored identically to three decimal places. The table looked like a finding and was an artifact. Alerts now carry arrival times spread over a week, in bursts, which is also what makes the coalescing figure mean anything.

The benchmark wrote its own clock, the wrong one. This package ships a virtual clock whose docstring explains at length why the naive version, a counter that each sleep advances by its own duration, serialises concurrent sleeps. The benchmark then wrote that exact naive version, and hedging measured as having no effect at all, because nothing was ever still outstanding when a hedge delay elapsed. The clock moved into the package so there is one of it.

The clock could not drive code that touches disk. A coroutine inside asyncio.to_thread, which is how the cache reaches SQLite, is parked on a future another thread will resolve rather than on virtual time, so the clock had nothing to advance and no way to tell that from a deadlock. It raised on the first replay with a deadlock report when the only thing happening was a disk read. It now distinguishes the two by progress rather than by a timeout, and takes an activity hook, because progress inside tasks it does not own, which is what a run of cache hits is, was invisible to it.

The workspace was reused, so a run inherited the last one's cache. One run served every lookup from a cache it had not populated, reported zero provider requests, and the derived lookups per day came out as infinity. That is how the bug announced itself; had the stream been slightly different it would have reported a merely flattering number instead and been believed.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Each experiment uses the simplest mechanism that answers its own question.

Quota and lifetime experiments use no latency model and no virtual clock. A request count does not depend on how long a request takes. The stream is replayed in arrival order, grouped into two second windows so the coalescer sees concurrent arrivals, with the cache's clock set to each window so lifetimes expire as days pass. Deterministic, and there is nothing in it to be wrong about.

The hedging experiment uses real asyncio and really sleeps the drawn delays, on a smaller sample, because it is the only one that needs time to pass. The virtual clock stays in the package, where the unit tests use it to check the rate limiter at window boundaries, which is what it is good at.

Every replay starts from an empty directory.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
More code than one harness, and each piece is small enough to read in one sitting. No experiment can be broken by a change made for a different one.

The honest cost: the hedging experiment now takes real wall clock time, roughly one second of it per five hundred lookups at the modelled latency, which is why it runs on a smaller sample than the others and why its percentiles carry the sample size next to them.

docs.title: The general lesson, since it recurred
docs.text:
A benchmark whose scaffolding is harder to trust than the code under test is not measuring anything. Three of the four faults above produced plausible numbers rather than crashes: identical lifetime scores, hedging having no effect, and an infinite capacity. Only the last was obviously absurd, and it was obvious by luck.

The same mistake also appeared twice in the library itself, in a form this ADR is the right place to name because it is the same error of reasoning. Both the coalescer and the hedger originally reported per call facts by comparing a shared counter before and after. Under concurrency that attributes other calls' work to this one: a burst of 25 reported 25 coalesced lookups out of 25, which is one more than can exist, and a hedging run reported 583 provider requests for 217 lookups, which is more than one hedge each and so impossible. Both now return what the call itself did. A counter delta is not a per call measurement, and the fact that it reads like one is the whole problem.
